newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish premier storms the centre ground.
newsitem.headline: Danish premier storms the centre ground.

text.p: Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen, mindful of polls showing the growing popularity of the Liberal opposition, unveiled on Tuesday a legislative programme to broaden the appeal of his Social Democrats.

In a speech opening of parliament Rasmussen addressed the worries of every sector of society, pledging better health and welfare services, a more just society, better education and more parish priests for the state-financed Lutheran church.
He called for less government form-filling for smaller businesses but closer state supervision of public pension funds.

Proposals specially likely to strike a chord with Liberal and Conservative voters include tighter immigration policy, new police powers to fight warring bike gangs and a proposal to reverse the burden of proof in major narcotics cases.

"Nyrup can no longer leave his right flank open. The voters are clearly to the right of the Social Democrat leadership on the question of law and order," political scientist Ole Borre told the Danish daily Politiken on Tuesday.

Rasmussen's minority coalition governnment is not due to seek re-election until 1998 but he is said to be concerned both by the Liberals' poll showings and by policy differences with one of his coalition partners, the centrist Radical Liberals.

A recent poll published in Politiken said that if an election were held now the Liberals would be the country's strongest single party, with 31.2 percent of the vote, while the Social Democrats trailed with 29.4 percent.
In the 1994 elections the Liberals won 23.3 percent and the Social Democrats 34.6 percent.

Journalist Lasse Ellegaard, author of a forthcoming book on the Social Democrats, agreed that the party could sink below 30 percent by 1998 unless Rasmussen could show "clear and visible" results in overhauling the health and welfare systems.

"Many of the Social Democrats' core voters are over 50 years of age, these are the issues about which they are deeply concerned," he told Reuters, adding that the party's goal of a balanced public sector budget in 1997 could be hard to attain.

"Many of their voters are public employees who could lose their jobs in public spending cuts. How do the Social Democrats stay in power and still make an effective reform of the public sector ? That is their dilemma," Ellegaard said.

Analysts say that the Social Democrats are themselves divided between Rasmussen's followers, who seek to move the party to the right and supporters of ousted party leader Svend Auken who want it to swing to the left, or at least stay put.
In addition, Rasmussen's private spats with the Radical Liberals -- who hold the foreign affairs, economy and education portfolios in his government -- are becoming more public.

The junior coalition partner did little to hide its irritation at not being consulted over the new law and order package and only receiving details late on Sunday evening and hinted that the measures would not be rubber-stamped when they reached parliament.
"Legislation by prime ministerial decree has not yet been introduced to Denmark," the Berlingske Tidende daily quoted a Radical Liberal source as saying.
